# The incoming branch is checked against its OWN audit log, not ours. That is not
# a technicality: a branch may add a user and have that user seal a secret, and
# our side has never heard of them until the log merge applies the tell. Checking
# against our log instead would reject that entirely legitimate branch.

sesam-repo admin base.txt mine.txt theirs.txt

cp $TMPDIR/base.txt s
exec sesam add s --group admin
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'add s'

# THEIRS: a new admin is told in, and that new user reseals the secret.
exec git checkout -b withbob
exec sesam tell --user bob --recipient $BOB_PUBKEY --group admin
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'tell bob'

cp $TMPDIR/theirs.txt s
env SESAM_ID=$BOB_KEY
exec sesam seal
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'bob reseals s'

# The object really is sealed by someone our branch does not know yet.
exec sesam show .sesam/objects/s.sesam
stdout 'THEIRS'
grep '"sealed_by":"bob"' .sesam/objects/s.sesam

# OURS: our own change to the same secret, so the driver has to merge it.
env SESAM_ID=$ADMIN_KEY
exec git checkout master
cp $TMPDIR/mine.txt s
exec sesam seal
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'ours: reseal s'

# Accepted: bob is vouched for by the log of the branch he sealed on.
! exec git merge withbob
stderr 'automatically merging revealed file s'
! stderr 'does not verify'
! stderr 'invalid signature'

cp $TMPDIR/mine.txt s
exec git add -A
exec git commit --no-edit
exec sesam verify
stderr 'Integrity: ok'

# Both the tell and the reseal survived the merge.
exec sesam user ls
stdout 'bob'

-- base.txt --
BASE
-- mine.txt --
MINE
-- theirs.txt --
THEIRS
